title: SEDD: Scalable and Efficient Dataset Deduplication with GPUs

problem.claim: Dataset deduplication is a crucial preprocessing step for improving data quality and large language model performance.

gap.claim: Existing GPU-accelerated deduplication frameworks remain suboptimal because of communication overhead from physical data shuffling and underutilized GPU resources.

contributions.claim: SEDD is a GPU-accelerated deduplication framework optimized for distributed cluster environments.
SEDD combines a partially reusable hash function, optimized GPU kernels, hardware-aware automatic parameter selection, and streaming-based processing.
SEDD reports substantially higher deduplication speed than CPU- and GPU-based baselines while maintaining high deduplication fidelity.

author_reported_evidence.claim: On 30 million documents processed with four GPUs, SEDD reportedly outperforms the SlimPajama CPU-based tool by up to 158× and the NVIDIA NeMo Curator GPU-based tool by up to 7.8×.
The MinHash signature generation phase reportedly achieves speedups of up to 375× over the CPU baseline.
The authors report deduplicating 1.2 trillion tokens in 3 hours on an 8-node, 32-GPU V100 cluster, with duplicate-set Jaccard similarities above 0.95 relative to standard MinHash.

narrative_sequence.summary: Dataset deduplication improves data quality and language-model performance, with MinHash LSH commonly used.
Existing GPU frameworks are limited by data-shuffling communication overhead and GPU underutilization.
SEDD addresses the gap through reusable hashing, optimized GPU kernels, hardware-aware tuning, and streaming instead of traditional shuffling.
The authors report large speedups, high similarity to standard MinHash results, and trillion-token-scale processing.
The related code is reported as publicly available on GitHub.

source_observation.claim: Replacing physical data shuffling with streaming is reported to mitigate communication bottlenecks.

interpretation.claim: Communication-aware data movement can be a central optimization target in distributed GPU preprocessing.

application.claim: When designing distributed GPU pipelines, evaluate streaming or locality-preserving alternatives to bulk data shuffling.

exception.claim: The abstract does not establish whether streaming is preferable for workloads or hardware configurations beyond those evaluated.

source_observation.claim: The reported system maintains Jaccard similarities above 0.95 relative to standard MinHash while improving processing speed.

interpretation.claim: Performance optimization can preserve close agreement with an established deduplication method.

application.claim: Assess accelerated preprocessing systems with both throughput metrics and agreement or fidelity measures.

exception.claim: The abstract does not specify the evaluation protocol, datasets, or thresholds used to determine duplicate sets.

unknowns: The abstract does not specify the datasets, corpus composition, or workload distribution used beyond the reported scales.
The abstract does not describe the experimental protocol, baseline configurations, or statistical variation.
The abstract does not provide implementation details for the hash function, GPU kernels, or parameter-selection mechanism.
